verdict: Caution on Delhi hospitals & diagnostics: lend selectively to cash-and-insurance-driven day-care and diagnostic chains, avoid CGHS-dependent facilities until empanelment is re-established.
title: Delhi hospitals & diagnostics: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business is and where cash sits
A hospital converts doctors, beds and equipment into billed procedures; a diagnostic chain converts samples into test reports. **Cash sits in the billing cycle, not the asset base** — hospitals carry heavy fixed cost (doctors, equipment, rent) and need occupancy to break even, while diagnostics run on volume and price per test. Peer data shows the tension: tests per patient rose 9.2% but average revenue per test fell 8.7% to Rs 357 [7]. So when a proposal lands, check payer mix first; if government-scheme billing is above a third, ask for the empanelment letter and renewal date.

## What has changed in Delhi now
**99 healthcare facilities across Delhi-NCR were de-empanelled under CGHS** because empanelment was not renewed [2]. That is a direct cash shock for any borrower whose receivables sit with CGHS. Against that, the local news is expansionary: Gut Clinic is widening its Delhi-NCR outpatient network with a policy push toward technology-driven healthcare [1], and a Fortis arm has signed to service a 400-bedded hospital in Delhi [3]. Peer results are strong — Aster DM's Q4 operating EBITDA rose 31% to Rs 253 crore with margins at 21.7% [5], and brokerages expect diagnostics volume growth through FY27 on stable pricing [4][6]. Note the rating reports are undated or old (ICRA methodology, Park Medi World October 2025) [9][11]; treat them as structural, not current.

## Where to grow
**Pursue day-care and specialty outpatient chains, diagnostic labs with B2C walk-in volumes, and service/management contracts on third-party hospital assets** — the Fortis-style servicing model [3] keeps capex off the borrower's books. Avoid pure CGHS-receivable facilities and single-doctor dependent clinics; ICRA flags doctor retention as critical under intense competition [10].

## How to grow safely
Structure against receivables, not projections. **Take monthly: billing by payer, days-sales-outstanding by insurer and scheme, occupancy or test volumes, and doctor attrition.** Covenant that CGHS/insurance receivables stay below an agreed share, and require the empanelment renewal letter as a condition. Hospitals carry significant reinvestment needs for expansion and upgradation [9], so size term debt to cash flow after maintenance capex.

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly payer-mix shift toward scheme billing -> ask for renewal status and hold new limits.
- Average revenue per test falling while volumes rise -> recheck pricing power and margin.
- Key doctor exits or occupancy dip -> reassess repayment capacity.
